question: What Happens to Checkout If My Payment Gateway Goes Down?
metaDescription: Customers using that specific gateway can't check out at all — a genuine outage is rare but worth planning for with at least one backup gateway active.
shortAnswer: If a gateway's API is unreachable, any customer trying to pay through it will see a checkout error, and no order will be created for that attempt — WooCommerce has no automatic fallback to a different gateway mid-transaction. A customer using a different, still-functioning gateway is unaffected, which is the strongest argument for offering more than one payment method rather than relying on a single provider.

bodyHtml:
Why There's No Automatic Fallback

Each payment gateway integration in WooCommerce operates independently — when a customer selects a gateway and submits payment, that specific gateway's API is called directly, with no built-in mechanism to detect a failure and silently retry through a different, unrelated gateway instead. A genuine full outage of a major provider (Stripe, PayPal) is rare, but does happen occasionally, and when it does, every customer relying on that gateway simply can't complete checkout until it's resolved.

What Actually Happens During an Outage

  • The customer sees a checkout error (often a fairly generic one, per how gateways handle failures) and no order is created for that specific attempt.
  • A customer with access to a different active gateway can simply select that instead and complete their order normally — this is the main practical mitigation available.
  • Status pages published by major gateways (Stripe's, PayPal's) are usually the fastest way to confirm whether an issue is on the gateway's side versus something local to the store.
  • A store with only one active gateway has no fallback at all during an outage, which is a meaningful business continuity risk worth weighing against the simplicity of a single-gateway setup.

Reducing the Risk

  1. Offer at least two independent gateways (ideally from different providers, not two integrations of the same underlying processor) so an outage on one doesn't block all checkouts.
  2. Monitor the active gateways' status pages or set up alerting, so an outage is caught quickly rather than discovered through a spike in support complaints.
  3. Have a clear communication plan (a checkout banner, a support response template) ready for a genuine outage, so customers aren't left confused during the (usually brief) disruption.
